where: the Tulm-Varo estate's boats on the channel north of Blackrose
what: Rows-For-Another holed one of the estate's boats and was assessed four nushmeekos, four months of work.

when: eleven years before, and the two years after
what: The estate's keeper of the count, a debtor hatched on the estate, wrote Rows-For-Another's leaf in a small exact hand, the four months, then her food, then a fever. That keeper was Never-Sold, before she was bought out.

Hulm-Tei, keeper after her, wrote every season's true lines in a larger hand; the leaf outgrew her. Whatever any leaf is short at the season's reckoning is written onto his own leaf, the last in the box; if his leaf is lost, the shortfall is spread over every hand on the estate. He keeps the box locked in the estate house and its key on him.

where: the channel north of the bank
what: Brings-Them-Back, the estate's fetcher, watches the channel for a head-price. He knows the way to every hand's home tree, so a runaway who lives can never go home while he lives.
Never-Sold wrote a false leaf ("worked, struck") in her small hand and put by the Owing's first price, 100 gold. She knows of the keeper's leaf and does not say so.

when: before the player came to Blackrose
where: the Rose, far to the north, and the heirs' post on Blackrose's east shore
what: A fire went through the Rose's upper cells. The heirs moved three of their held to the outer post under one gate-keeper, Third-Born Tsaxi, who counts heads and cannot read.

where: the swamp tent in the western swamp
what: The Rose's reckoner, who alone reads the singed leaves that say why each is held, came north by the wet road round the west of the lake with four men; beasts took them at his camp. His strongbox, with the leaves, his seal ring and his dagger, lies in his tent; a lamia keeps the place.

Mends-Nets drowned the heirs' shelter-reckoner Otheel in a net after he added a third winter to Seven-Floods' roof-owing. Mends-Nets is to be put under, sent below to the dead levels, when the leaf is read.
Walks-Far said before the whole yard that the gate to the dead levels should be opened and the Rose left. He owes three seasons for it. Both younger held can recite his words, and both claim them.

Seven-Floods, Rows-For-Another's mother, owes the heirs for a roof and always will; the smoke is in her chest; she wants to die near her Hist, and she wants Mends-Nets, who killed for her, to go first. She knows who is who and will not say lightly.

Ussa-Rekh bought Owings out and carved a token for each person, kept until they had worked one season's hire for him, which paid for the next person bought. One year a berth-master paid for a whole freed crew's season and it bought twenty people out; since then the seasons have had a way of becoming two. He keeps nothing for himself.

Heavy-Rope's crew have worked their season and one more; their tokens are still in the Broker's chest. Ra'Jhan pays this season's hire when it is sailed, and it is promised to the price of eleven people held at Thorn, whose names he keeps.

Ussa-Rekh bought out the Tulm-Varo estate's keeper of the count for the price of a boat. She took the name Never-Sold and refused the bound count he offered her; it is on his shelf, and the first leaf copied into it is Rows-For-Another's, in her small exact hand.
Feldril Nethri, a Dunmer working off months at Soulrest, is put by the Broker's north door and keeps it barred.

when: before the well was dug, and every year since
what: The landing digs its plaster clay at a cut bank where the river swings west below the ford, on the station bank outside its walls. It was the landing's cut before the Imperials came, and the station has never claimed it. The landing renews the clay of its walls every dry season, and its clay work is renewed the same way.

when: the years since the well was dug
what: The Imperials set the well's stone head and lining in the clay bank by the ford. The bank moves with every monsoon, and the lining cracks. Each dry season Livia Varinius re-mortars the cracks herself, with a trowel and a tub of mortar she keeps under the windlass cover. Everyone can see the well head is cracked; nobody at the station knows the lining has cracked and been mended every year. Livia believes a mason's proper new lining will hold where her mortar did not; the lining was Imperial masons' work from the start and has cracked every year since.

when: 5 Rain's Hand, 4E 201 (the ledger page), early this dry season
what: A new crack opens a finger wide from the coping down the lining, on the side that faces the ford, below the water line, beside the old mortar lines. Livia writes it in the station ledger in the old log's order (time, count, state).

Ford water seeps through the lining below ground, and fine silt with it. The morning bucket comes up with silt in the bottom, and the water tastes of the ford. Livia keeps the silt in a jar under the windlass cover, beside her trowel and mortar tub, to show a mason when one comes. She gives a dipper of the well's water to any traveller who has paid the stop.

Livia asks the landing to haul stone for a new lining. Signs-For-The-Cargo refuses. The landing does not build in stone, and it does not drink the well's water; its households draw from the well only to wash.

when: this season, before the ledger page
what: Each bank has always charged for its own half of the stop. Livia raises the station's charge from one drake to two for every traveller who stops, for the stop and its water, to pay a mason from Gideon to re-line the well in stone. She charges the landing's people nothing for water, as she always has.

when: a few days after t5, before 3 Rain's Hand
what: In answer, Signs-For-The-Cargo begins to charge walkers who wade the ford one drake a head; before, only carts on the raft paid. He says the ford was worked before the well was dug. Travellers ask Livia why the landing charges them again, and she writes that in the ledger too.

Some travellers who have paid at the station slip out at night along the station bank, past the clay cut, and wade the shallow tail of the river below the pool, out of the poler's sight, to dodge the landing's charge. They leave prints in the clay of the cut.

when: ten days before the player comes
what: A crocodile, drawn by the offal from the drying racks and the night waders, takes the deep pool under the cut. It comes up at Signs-For-The-Cargo while he digs plaster clay. He drops the clay basket at the cut and runs. Nobody has dug there since. The station house has no watch post and nobody at the station hunts, so the crocodile has been left alone.

when: now, late in the dry season
what: The rains are close. The landing must replaster its walls before them and has no clay. Takes-The-Short-Weight, who judges everything by its water and keeps a bucket of ford water by her door, told the poler the walkers' charge is wrong and is sending travellers to the crocodile; he would not hear it.

when: every dry season, and early this one
what: The poler's wife draws wash water at the well (the ledger page, 4 Rain's Hand). She has watched Livia at the coping with a trowel every dry season, and this season saw her lift the windlass cover and put silt in a jar. She told Takes-The-Short-Weight.
Ahzi-Tal, a Helstrom courier, lodges for one night. Reeh-Shaal, who pays for her bed in salt and travels the same road, sees that his satchel holds a sealed packet his ledger does not list.
Reeh-Shaal buys a length of rope from Tsono-Ra after the lodge has closed, saying she needs it to tie her pack.

Reeh-Shaal kills Ahzi-Tal at the stone lip, takes the satchel, ties the body's wrists and pins it with a grave-stake in the spring's throat under the Hist's roots, so it will not float up. She leaves the stake's face uncarved.
Haj-Tei finds the courier's bed empty, his pack still in the lodge store and his bill unpaid. He decides the courier left before dawn without paying and keeps the pack against the debt.
The body fouls the water. Guests who drink it, or eat food cooked in it, fall sick with fever and retching.
Reeh-Shaal stays at the lodge, saying she waits for a boat to Helstrom. She waits for the packet's buyer, who has not come, and tells the sick guests it is the fire stand's food.
After the lamps are out, Reeh-Shaal goes to the stone lip and looks down into the water for a while, to be sure the body has not come up. Haj-Tei has seen her there from the lodge door.

Wuleen-Taza, who does the landing crew's bargaining, began dumping fish offal from the crew's bait bucket into the shallows east of the scaffold at night, and the crew spread word of a beast in the deep channel that Sells-Dear's boat runs and no raft needs, so that traders would keep off her boat and take the crew's rafts; Okan-Zish knew and kept quiet.

where: the shallows east of the scaffold
what: The offal drew a real crocodile up the river; it made its lair in the shallows east of the scaffold and took one of the crew's rafts. The crew left the bucket in the shallows, afraid to go down for it.

where: the landing, on the rock roots
what: Okan-Zish, afraid of the beast now that it is real, wants it killed and says nothing of the bait until it is dead.

when: three days before the player came
where: the road at the city's edge
what: Sei-Wan walked out of the town into the basin alone, east past the houses, to prove himself to Helstrom's Agaceph; a walk-out ends when the walker comes back on his own feet.

where: the dry ground in the basin of the basin east of the road
what: On his way back a viper struck at him out among the trees; he has stayed on the dry ground since, because it lies south-west of him, and he has no weapon that can reach it.
Haj-Wan waits by the road; the custom of Sei-Wan's tribe, the Agaceph, forbids its own to follow a walk-out, and the levy warden keeps the road and leaves a tribe's rite to that tribe.

where: the lower channel below Nine Bends, then the estuary bank above Lilmoth
what: The months of an Owing gang and their families were sold on from the lower channel to Buys-The-Months, a Lilmoth debt-labour broker, who hires the gang out to unload the lighters at Lilmoth's dock and keeps their months on his work roll. The families lodge at a camp on the estuary bank a night's rowing above Lilmoth, and so as not to wash out far from their tree they planted a cutting of Nine Bends' Hist there, with their clutch at its roots (QA1). Ux-Xeek is his port hand, who calls the gang out to the lighters. Dives-Without-A-Rope, of a family that answers to Nine Bends, has thinned in colour from her years away from it.

Cuts-the-Old-Knot learns that the state's courier, Mee-Tuja, will come down to Lilmoth with the broker's gang from its camp, as cover, carrying a sealed satchel for the Veiled Reed's handler in Lilmoth, and that the camp keeps a small Hist cutting.

where: the gang's camp on the estuary bank
what: Her cell comes in off the water. She kills Mee-Tuja and takes the satchel; two of her people cut the cutting's roots from the clutch and draw its sap into jars they brought; the huts burn and the eggs die. A stranger lies hurt by the fire, on no roll and known to nobody there; she looks at the stranger and leaves them alive. How the stranger came to the bank nobody at the camp knows.

Wuleen-Sei, the broker's overseer, gets the gang into its longboat and down the estuary through the night to the broker's ship, moored at the broker's ship, moored below Hereguard Plantation, west of Lilmoth, where the gang sleeps in the hold. Dives-Without-A-Rope carries the hurt stranger aboard, and a jar one of the cutters dropped by the fire.

where: Salts-The-Catch's house and the broker's ship
what: Nesh-Deeka waits at the house Salts-The-Catch keeps for the Reed (QA8) for a courier who does not come. When the ship comes in without him, Salts-The-Catch, who sells the broker his gang's food, asks him for anyone off the ship who saw the camp burn, for whom her guest, Nesh-Deeka, will pay. The broker tells her of the jar and the stranger, and keeps his own hands, who are his months. The broker passes on what his overseer told him: the woman with the knotted cord had the cutting cut from its eggs, and looked at the stranger by the fire and let them live.

The stranger wakes in the hold. Buys-The-Months stands on the deck of the ship. The stranger's name is on no line of his roll, so they owe him nothing and he cannot hire them out; he wants them off his ship.

when: years before, and since the camp burned
what: Nesh-Deeka handles the Veiled Reed's hands in Lilmoth for the An-Xileel's offices at Stormhold, the state's city in the north-west (10-political-frame §5; 36-cast-roster §55), and answers to them, not to any tree, village or court. The Reed watches for cults, smugglers and killers who would harm the state or the trees (10-political-frame §6), works through houses like Salts-The-Catch's and wears no mark (QA8). Its deniable hands are people nobody can claim: if one is taken, the Reed never knew them. Mee-Tuja, the courier, was one, walking with debt gangs as cover; since he died at the camp, the Reed has claimed neither his body nor his name. The Reed puts fifty gold in a new hand's palm when they say yes. Nesh-Deeka tells new hands plainly that she keeps two things from them, and names neither (36-cast-roster §55).

when: two nights before the game opens
where: the gang's camp on the estuary bank
what: Two of the cell's people came off the water with empty jars, cut the cutting's roots at the clutch and filled the jars from the cut roots; one jar, filled and stoppered, rolled from a cutter's arm by the fire and was left when the cell went back to the water (MQ01 t2).

Dives-Without-A-Rope, whose family answers to Nine Bends, the cutting's parent, picked up the jar and carried it aboard with the hurt stranger. She keeps it in a lockbox she keeps locked, with the key on her, meaning to lick the sap and hear her tree once before it is taken from her. She has not dared taste it yet; twenty gold would be a month off her roll. Ux-Xeek's spare picks for the lighters' padlocks lie loose on the hold's floor by the lockbox.

Nesh-Deeka, told of the jar by Salts-The-Catch from the broker, sends the Reed's new hand for it. She has heard that sap shows a taster visions, and that a stranger tastes it differently; she means to have the stranger taste it and to write down whatever they say. The same day word reaches her that the Hist of Low-Reed Village, east of Lilmoth, has turned its face.

when: when the player tastes the sap
what: The sap holds the player for some breaths. They speak of the ship's hold, empty, with roots grown up through its deck in a ring like trees, and a door at the top of its stairs that is not the ship's door and that nobody built, and a dry voice in it that makes no words; on a stranger the sap leaves a dry anger that passes (QA18). Nesh-Deeka writes it down and gives the page to the player. What it means stays unexplained (§18d).
Cuts-the-Old-Knot sends two of her cell, Hides-His-Wake and Counts-The-Jars, each with the knotted cord at the wrist, to cut a tended Hist with a village round it and draw its sap into jars.

where: the village's stores and the Hist's roots under the stilts
what: While Pays-Late, the tree-minder, is out on the water with the netters, the two men pole in from the north reeds, take his knife from his things, cut a root of the Hist under the stilts, draw its sap into jars, seal the cut with the village's black gum and pole away north. Turns-The-Clutch, at the egg pool, sees a boat come in from the north reeds and go back out, and takes it for a netter.
The Hist turns its face, its light out and its leaves shut; the cut severs the eggs from the tree and they die. The sap weeping at the cut draws the leech water's leeches to the root (QA11).

Pays-Late finds the root cut and sealed with his own gum and his knife gone. Knowing it will look like his work, he tells only Turns-The-Clutch, keeps his gum pot locked in a box at his feet, and stands on the bank from then on.
The village sees the leeches and blames them, and blames Pays-Late, whose keeping the tree is; it sees him stand on the bank day and night.

where: a giant tree's roots in the north reeds, past the leech water
what: The two men keep the jars at a giant tree's roots deep in the north reeds, past the leech water and out of sight of the village's last huts, waiting for the cell's larger boat, and fight anyone who comes near.

The player saw a Hist whose root the cell cut and whose sap it drew into jars; its eggs died of the cut. A Hist that falls silent kills no clutch (hist-and-sap), so a cut is a different thing from a silence.
Nesh-Deeka decides that the interior's tree-minders and Nisswo, who gather at Helstrom and carry news home, must hear what a cut Hist looks like from someone the Reed can deny. She sends no escort.

where: the marsh way between Helstrom's landing and the paved road
what: Two giant wasps nest at the way's far bend, where the way runs over a root, and set on anyone who comes near.

where: among the trees by the stone towers
what: Kaska-Meen and Ei-Tuja stand near each other among the trees by the stone towers; they read a silent Hist differently, and have said so to each other before: she holds that it must be watched by tree-minders alone, he that its silence is its own act, to be read and not clamped. Neither has seen a cut root.
The levy warden by the paved road warns strangers that what walks into the basin round Helstrom dies (LQ30's road).
Tree-minders and Nisswo know what a dying Hist leaves, a Mnemic Egg of its sap and memories, and that the Dominion once used one to stop a generation of eggs hatching (hist-and-sap, Mnemic Egg).

In a dry year the founders went down the root galleries and cut a channel from a brine seam toward the roots of a rival grove downstream, to sour its water and take its travellers. The rival grove withered; Greenspring grew.
The founders carved the descent on their own grave-stakes in the old way, as a deed done for the tribe, and never spoke of it to outsiders.
With the grove downstream dead, the channel silted on that side; each flood now pushes the brine back up the cut into Greenspring's own taproots.
Vees-Wai finds the Hist's leaves falling out of season and the sap thin. The village tastes salt in the spring and blames the salt works upstream.
Ixo-Vaal stopped trading for salt-works salt when the works closed their landing; he now buys upriver rock salt, which he keeps in a sack at his door.
S'Tabi sells to the Chapter and sends those who ask for quiet work to Tilts-The-Jug inside the house.

Keeps-What-Floats took a necklace of polished blue jaspers from a sleeping Lookout of the Chapter on the dock, and locked it in his own strongbox by the houses at the water's edge; he keeps the key on him. He is a coward and runs from any fight, and he has no buyer for it yet.
Tilts-The-Jug decides to see how the newcomer works: the Lookout's necklace is to come back with no harm done to the one who took it.
Keeps-What-Floats idles on the shore by the houses with Sits-By-The-Water, who is his friend and does not think much of him.
The Chapter meets under Lilmoth, reached by a trapdoor on a ruin standing in the deep water east of Lilmoth; Bent-Spine, its fence, keeps to the inner room.

where: the deep water east of Lilmoth
what: A merchant who took pledges against loans drowned crossing the deep water east of Lilmoth with his lockbox. His body was brought out; the lockbox, locked and too heavy, lies on the floor where he went down.
Bent-Spine wants what is in the lockbox before the clients find a diver, and leaves to the newcomer what becomes of it, to see their judgement.

where: the south bank of the deep water
what: Three of the merchant's clients are on the south bank, each with a claim on one thing in the box, and each claim is a lie.
The statue is worn smooth by many hands over many years; the merchant had the charm set in a new silver mount of his own; the beads are Kothringi glass, the kind the old cairns hold.
